findings.title: MRC.exe — temporally impossible DLL timestamps (anti-forensic timestomping)

peirce_chain.firstness: MRC.exe (PID=29440) running from D:\Tools\MRC.exe. Written in Visual Basic 6 (MSVBVM60.DLL). 32-bit process on 64-bit system (Wow64=True). Base address 0x400000 — compiled without ASLR. ALL DLL LoadTime timestamps range from 1600-12-01 to 1718-02-19. Launched 83 seconds before memory dump. Parent: explorer.exe (user-launched).
peirce_chain.secondness: DLL LoadTime timestamps predating the FILETIME epoch (1601-01-01) are TEMPORALLY IMPOSSIBLE. No legitimate software — including forensic acquisition tools — produces LoadTime values in the 1600-1718 range. This is either FILETIME zeroing (all 64 bits of the FILETIME structure set to near-zero) or deliberate timestomping. FILETIME zeroing across ALL DLLs is a systematic anti-forensic technique, not random corruption. VB6, no-ASLR, non-standard path (D:\Tools\), and unsigned binary compound the anomaly. No legitimate modern tool combines all these characteristics.
peirce_chain.thirdness: Deliberate anti-forensic concealment. The actor systematically zeroed DLL LoadTime timestamps to prevent timeline reconstruction. This is a T1070.006 (Timestomp) technique — a hallmark of MALICE because it demonstrates awareness of forensic analysis and active measures to defeat it. The concealment layer elevates this from INTENT (did something deliberate) to MALICE (is hiding that they did it). Corroborated by F-002 (injection) and F-003 (C2) forming a coherent three-stage attack chain.

findings.carnegie_pattern: Authority transfer — binary name 'MRC.exe' and placement in 'D:\Tools\' mimics a legitimate tool to reduce analyst suspicion
findings.devil_advocate: MRC.exe COULD be a legitimate but poorly written forensic memory acquisition tool. VB6-era tools exist in forensics (e.g., MoonSols DumpIt predecessors). Some memory acquisition tools produce LoadTime artifacts because they zero certain structures during the dump process. The D:\Tools\ path could be an examiner's toolkit drive. HOWEVER: (1) no known acquisition tool zeros ALL DLL LoadTimes to pre-epoch values — this is not a documented acquisition artifact; (2) legitimate acquisition tools are signed or have known vendor provenance; (3) the temporal impossibility spans centuries (1600-1718), not a simple epoch error; (4) the presence of concurrent shellcode injection (F-002) and C2 (F-003) means MRC.exe exists alongside active compromise artifacts, not in isolation.
findings.corroboration: CONFIRMED by functional chain: F-002 (shellcode injection in SearchApp.exe) + F-003 (C2 from SearchFilterHost) demonstrate active compromise. MRC.exe timestomping provides the concealment layer. Three independent Volatility plugins (dlllist, malfind, netscan) across three processes.

findings.title: SearchApp.exe shellcode injection — trampolining code in RWX regions

peirce_chain.firstness: SearchApp.exe (PID=8312) has 4 PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE memory regions not backed by files on disk. Region 0x255fe730000 contains byte sequence 48 B8 xx xx xx xx 48 FF E0 followed by CC (INT3) padding.
peirce_chain.secondness: PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE regions not backed by disk files are the primary indicator of code injection. The byte sequence 48 B8 (MOV RAX, imm64) + FF E0 (JMP RAX) is a TRAMPOLINING SHELLCODE STUB — a position-independent code redirection technique. INT3 (0xCC) padding is the standard shellcode NOP equivalent. This is NOT JIT compilation: JIT engines (CLR, V8, Chakra) use different patterns, do not produce MOV RAX;JMP RAX trampolines, and their regions are typically backed by JIT caches. SearchApp.exe is a UWP app with no legitimate reason for position-independent shellcode. FOUR separate regions indicate multi-stage injection, not a single allocation anomaly.
peirce_chain.thirdness: Process injection (T1055) into a Windows Search component. The attacker chose SearchApp.exe because: (1) it is a persistent UWP process that is always running, (2) it shares the Search subsystem with SearchFilterHost (the C2 channel in F-003), (3) UWP processes have network access capabilities. The injection technique (trampolining) is sophisticated — it redirects execution flow through absolute address jumps, enabling payload execution in the context of a trusted process. This is Living-off-the-Land Binary (LOLBIN) exploitation of the Windows Search stack.

findings.carnegie_pattern: Trust exploitation — injecting into a Microsoft-signed UWP process to inherit its trust and network permissions
findings.devil_advocate: SearchApp.exe is a UWP application that uses the Edge WebView2 runtime. Some UWP apps allocate RWX memory for JavaScript JIT compilation (Chakra/V8). HOWEVER: (1) the specific byte pattern MOV RAX;JMP RAX is not a JIT compiler output — it is a shellcode trampoline; (2) INT3 padding is a shellcode convention, not a JIT convention; (3) FOUR separate regions with this pattern exceed any reasonable JIT false-positive threshold; (4) the functional link to SearchFilterHost C2 (F-003) corroborates malicious use.
findings.corroboration: CONFIRMED by F-003 (SearchFilterHost C2 to Azure). Injection staging in SearchApp + C2 channel from SearchFilterHost = coherent attack chain within the Windows Search subsystem. Two independent Volatility plugins (malfind + netscan).

habit_incongruence.confirmed_by: Corroboration with F-003 (C2 channel in sibling Search process)

findings.shannon_entropy: N/A — shellcode byte patterns analyzed structurally, not by entropy

findings.title: SearchFilterHost.exe anomalous C2 to Microsoft Azure

peirce_chain.firstness: SearchFilterHost.exe (PID=24920) has TCP ESTABLISHED connection to 52.113.194.132:443 (Microsoft Azure). Connection active at 2020-11-16 02:33:38 UTC — during memory acquisition. DLL list incomplete (4 modules only).
peirce_chain.secondness: SearchFilterHost.exe is a subprocess of SearchIndexer.exe. Its SOLE function is loading filter handler DLLs to parse local document content for indexing. It does NOT initiate ANY external network connections under ANY normal operating condition. Windows telemetry, update checks, and cloud sync are handled by dedicated service hosts (svchost, OneDrive, etc.), NEVER by SearchFilterHost. An ESTABLISHED TCP connection to an Azure IP from this process is a STRUCTURAL IMPOSSIBILITY in normal operation. Additionally, the incomplete DLL list (only 4 modules) suggests module enumeration interference — consistent with injection or hollowing that corrupts the PEB module list.
peirce_chain.thirdness: Command-and-control channel (T1071.001) using cloud infrastructure for traffic blending (T1102). The attacker chose SearchFilterHost because: (1) it is a trusted Microsoft-signed process, (2) security tools rarely monitor it for network activity, (3) Azure destination (52.113.194.132) blends with legitimate Microsoft traffic, making network-level detection difficult. The C2 channel is functionally linked to the injection staging in SearchApp.exe (F-002) — the attacker used the Search subsystem as both injection host and communication channel. This is a sophisticated Living-off-the-Cloud technique.

findings.carnegie_pattern: Traffic blending — using Microsoft Azure infrastructure to make C2 traffic indistinguishable from legitimate Microsoft cloud communication
findings.devil_advocate: 52.113.194.132 is a Microsoft Azure IP. Windows 10 components occasionally connect to Microsoft cloud services in unexpected ways, especially after feature updates. SearchFilterHost COULD theoretically load a cloud-aware filter handler that initiates a connection. HOWEVER: (1) no documented Windows 10 behavior has SearchFilterHost initiating external connections; (2) the connection is ESTABLISHED (not SYN_SENT or transient); (3) incomplete DLL enumeration suggests process-level interference; (4) direct functional link to shellcode injection in sibling process SearchApp.exe (F-002) eliminates the benign hypothesis.
findings.corroboration: CONFIRMED by F-002 (shellcode injection in SearchApp.exe, sibling process in Search subsystem). Two independent Volatility plugins. Attack chain: SearchApp (staging) -> SearchFilterHost (C2).

habit_incongruence.confirmed_by: Corroboration with F-002 (injection in sibling Search process)

findings.title: Cloud sync exfiltration surface — 5 services active simultaneously

peirce_chain.firstness: Five cloud sync processes active: OneDrive (PID 9648), Google Drive Sync (PID 8432), iCloudDrive (PID 13260), iCloudPhotos (PID 12532), Slack (PID 1152). All with established connections to respective cloud endpoints.
peirce_chain.secondness: Multiple cloud sync services on a single endpoint is unusual but not unprecedented for users who span ecosystems (Windows + macOS + Google). All services have legitimate autostart configurations. However, in context of active compromise (F-001/F-002/F-003), these services represent high-value exfiltration channels — an attacker with code execution could weaponize any of them.
peirce_chain.thirdness: The cloud services are not themselves compromised. They represent EXFILTRATION SURFACE — potential channels that an attacker could exploit. No evidence of anomalous data transfer through these channels was found.

findings.devil_advocate: All five cloud services have legitimate autostart and are commonly used together by users with multiple device ecosystems. Their presence is not evidence of exfiltration activity. Without observing anomalous upload volumes, staged data, or modified sync configurations, this is surface risk only.
findings.corroboration: No corroborating exfiltration evidence. Remains surface-level risk assessment.
